title: Registration week grows into a street dance and two mini-concerts
body: ASG expanded its registration week programme in autumn 1972 to include a street dance and two mini-concerts. The Talisman counted this among the activities of the Activities Committee under vice president Mike Fiorella.

title: ASG activity card goes on sale
body: The Herald announced that the ASG activity card was available. The Talisman described it as a programme begun two years earlier that admitted part-time students and the spouses of students to ASG activities for a nominal charge.

title: Chicago plays a free concert
body: ASG presented Chicago on 4 October 1972 as a free concert, with pianist Robert Lamm fronting the horn section. The Talisman called it one of the season's hottest entertainment nights and said the band was soon forgotten once Jethro Tull arrived three weeks later.

title: Buffalo Bob Smith revives the Howdy Doody show in Van Meter
body: ASG brought Buffalo Bob Smith and his revival of the Howdy Doody show to Van Meter Auditorium in October 1972. The Talisman called the two-and-a-half hour programme professional and a huge success, with Smith leading a rendition of 'Clarabell the Clown' and playing Chopin, Mozart and Bach.

title: Jethro Tull sells tickets and loses money
body: Ian Anderson brought Jethro Tull to Diddle Arena on 26 October 1972. Many in the audience called it the best concert ever staged at Western, but the Talisman recorded that the pay concert was a major financial loss for ASG.
money: a major financial loss for ASG, amount not stated

title: Pat Paulsen opens the lecture programme at Homecoming
body: ASG sponsored the political comedian Pat Paulsen on the evening of 1 November 1972, in Homecoming week, with a lecture titled 'Pat Paulsen Looks at the 70's'. The Talisman recorded that ASG's lecture programme for the year began with him.

title: The Beach Boys disappoint on Homecoming Friday
body: ASG sponsored the Beach Boys in Diddle Arena on Friday 3 November 1972. Students had come to hear the music of the sixties and heard little of it; the Talisman reported the concert was not well received until the band turned to its golden oldies, and that many went home disappointed.

title: ASG Homecoming Dance closes the day
body: The ASG Homecoming Dance in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom concluded the full day of Homecoming activities on 4 November 1972. It followed the game against Middle Tennessee and the reception in Diddle Arena.

title: Orphan plays a mini-concert to a poor crowd
body: The rock band Orphan played an ASG mini-concert on the Wednesday night of 15 November 1972. Al Cross reviewed it for the Herald under the headline that Orphan gave a bad crowd good music.

title: ASG loses money on the fall concerts
body: Al Cross reported in the Herald that ASG had lost money on its fall concerts. The Talisman confirmed the loss on fall entertainment without giving a figure, and the shortfall shaped the argument over the head fee that ran into the spring.
money: loss on fall concerts, figure not given in the sources consulted

title: Four free mini-concerts and the Cellar coffee house
body: ASG provided four free mini-concerts over the year, by Voice of Cheese, Tiny Alice, Orphan, and Rolfe Kempf with David McHugh. Weekend performances at the Cellar coffee house in West Hall rounded out the music ASG offered; the Talisman counted seven mini-concerts across the year in all.

title: The ASG Newsletter finally appears
body: After two years in the planning stages, the ASG Newsletter began publication with the November 1972 issue. It came out monthly and was meant to keep students aware of what was happening on campus.

title: ASG takes up the idea of a Free University
body: The Herald reported that ASG would consider establishing a Free University. The programme of no-cost, no-credit evening courses in subjects such as knitting, photography and yoga began the following spring under coordinator Glenn Jackson.

title: ASG schedules a venereal disease symposium
body: ASG scheduled a symposium on venereal disease, run in cooperation with Operation Venus and billed as 'V.D. Day'. The Talisman recorded that it was open to Western students, high school students and the public.

title: ASG announces a book exchange
body: The Herald reported that ASG would begin a book exchange. Congress had passed a bill to initiate a textbook exchange on campus, and the exchange ran at the start of the spring semester.

title: Student discount programme runs a sixth year
body: ASG's student discount programme continued for a sixth year, contracting with Bowling Green merchants who gave discounts to students. Plans were made to return to a discount coupon book alongside the discount card to increase use of the service.

title: Dance opens the spring season to two-thirds of a ballroom
body: ASG opened the spring semester on 2 February 1973 with the rock group Dance in the Garrett Ballroom. The Talisman said the mixture of blues-soul, Latin rock and hard rock made it hard to stay seated, but no more than two-thirds of the seats were filled.

title: Few attend the ASG symposiums
body: The Herald reported that few students attended the ASG symposiums. The venereal disease symposium had been the flagship of the series.

title: Stevie Wonder draws 3,850 and costs ASG up to $5,000
body: ASG presented Stevie Wonder with Billy Paul and Whole Oats as the first major concert of the second semester, on Tuesday 13 February 1973. The reviews said Wonder was wondrous, but only 3,850 were on hand and ASG lost between $4,000 and $5,000.

title: Buckminster Fuller lectures on 'Humans in the Universe'
body: The University Lecture Series and ASG jointly sponsored Buckminster Fuller, who spoke on 'Humans in the Universe' on 27 February 1973. The same joint series brought Steve Atlas of Nader's Raiders, who addressed about forty-five ASG Congress members and other interested people.

title: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan speak on the joint lecture series
body: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan were both sponsored by the 1972-73 University Lecture Series and ASG. King lectured on excerpts from her book on men's freedoms and their responsibilities; Friedan, called the mother superior of women's lib, spoke on women's liberation. The Talisman does not date either lecture.

title: Free University adds seven classes
body: The Herald reported that the Free University planned to add seven new classes. The programme of free evening courses was in its first semester.

title: Ron Beck calls a concert a mistake
body: Al Cross reported in the Herald that Ron Beck, the assistant dean of student affairs who handled concert booking, called a concert a mistake. Beck's judgment on which acts belonged on campus was the standing constraint on ASG's programme for the rest of the decade.

title: Congress votes a referendum on raising the head fee
body: ASG Congress voted to hold a student referendum on raising the head fee, a week after a Herald editorial argued the fee needed a boost to insure the quality of ASG entertainment. The regents instead voted an increase in ASG's allotment that August.

title: Lester Flatt headlines the Bluegrass Festival
body: ASG closed its season on 29 April 1973 with a Bluegrass and Folk Crafts Festival headlined by Lester Flatt and the Nashville Grass, with Mac Wiseman and II Generation. It was the second consecutive year the festival had been held.

title: An $11,000 budget increase pays for the concert and lecture year
body: The Board of Regents approved an $11,000 increase in the student affairs budget allocated to ASG in place of a proposed head fee rise. President Steve Yater said the increase was better than a higher head fee because it took no additional money from students' pockets, and the Talisman credited it with paying for the Doobie Brothers, Seals and Crofts and the mini-concerts.

title: Street dance and Ginger open the year at the amphitheatre
body: ASG began the year with the traditional street dance during registration week, then followed a few days later with the rock band Ginger in a mini-concert at the outdoor amphitheatre. It was the first outdoor performance at the fine arts amphitheatre and the first of the year's mini-concert series.

title: Stringbean headlines the second Bluegrass Festival
body: The second Bluegrass Festival was held on 6 September 1973 with the Hee Haw star Stringbean and other Nashville acts. The Herald reported five days later that a country-western 'git-together' had replaced the bluegrass festival.

title: Ethos plays the second mini-concert
body: The electronic-rock group Ethos from Fort Wayne, Indiana, played ASG's second mini-concert on 13 October 1973 in Van Meter Auditorium. Guitarist Bill Sharpe told the boogie-oriented audience that most of the boogies would have to be in their noses; the band was warmly received and returned in the spring as an off-campus support act.

title: Homecoming rock and roll revival: Jerry Lee Lewis cancels and Chuck Berry never shows
body: ASG's first attempt at a major concert, a 1950s Rock and Roll Revival for Homecoming, collapsed twice. Jerry Lee Lewis was first booked and cancelled over management problems, Chuck Berry was signed in his place and then took an unscheduled holiday in Las Vegas and ignored the date, leaving Gary U.S. Bonds to headline with the Crystals, Freddie Cannon and Lloyd Price. Ron Beck warned the crowd before the show and offered refunds to anyone who left within fifteen minutes, and he and ASG were still trying to recover the refund money from producer Richard Nader months later.

title: Red Snapper plays the ASG Homecoming dance
body: The Homecoming dance sponsored by ASG ran from 8pm to midnight after the game against Morehead, with music by Red Snapper. Homecoming 1973 took its theme from the movies and drew a crowd of 19,500 to the game in the rain.

title: A student takes the concert complaints to Congress
body: Tony Agee, a junior from Albany, brought his and his friends' grievances before the ASG Congress at the meeting of 29 October 1973. He charged that ASG had misrepresented facts, used false advertising and put incompetent people in charge of booking; president Steve Yater blamed the producer of the Homecoming revival.

title: Amnesty is the least successful mini-concert of the series
body: The soul-blues-jazz combo Amnesty played a mini-concert in Van Meter. The Talisman said much of the crowd enjoyed it but that it was the least successful show of the mini-concert series.

title: The Doobie Brothers play to 6,000
body: The Doobie Brothers played Diddle Arena on 4 December 1973 before a crowd of 6,000. The group had originally been booked for October and was postponed over a recording commitment; the Herald called the show average but the Talisman said it pleased most of the crowd.

title: Seals and Crofts play the first free concert in more than a year
body: Seals and Crofts opened the spring semester on Saturday 19 January 1974 before one of the largest crowds ever to see a show in Diddle Arena. The Talisman called it in some ways the best campus concert in more than a year and the first free concert since the autumn of 1972, scheduling and money having prevented one since.

title: The Free University shuts down after two semesters
body: The Herald reported that the Free U had shut down after two semesters. Coordinator Glenn Jackson blamed a lack of student interest and the difficulty of finding people to teach the classes, which had covered knitting, photography, yoga and other subjects.

title: ASG considers ending the legal loan fund
body: The Herald reported that ASG might end its legal loan fund. The Legal Rights Committee had been working towards a bail-bond fund for arrested students and had taken up drug expulsions, the refusal to show X-rated films in the student center and the 'Fly' censorship case.

title: Raymond McNally lectures on Dracula
body: ASG brought Dr Raymond McNally of Boston College, co-author of 'In Search of Dracula', to lecture on vampirism before a large audience in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom. He traced the legend to a fifteenth century Romanian prince and showed clips from vampire films.

title: Harry Chapin opens the major-mini concert series
body: ASG scheduled the folk singer and balladeer Harry Chapin for two shows in Van Meter on 3 March 1974. Activities vice president Tom LaCivita called it the first example of his new concept of major-mini concerts, in which medium-priced performers were brought in, sometimes free and sometimes as a pay event.

title: Herald calls the lecture series ASG's best effort to date
body: The Herald judged ASG's 1973-74 lecture series its best effort yet. The series had carried Senator Barry Goldwater, former attorney general Elliot Richardson and Senator Edmund Muskie, and ASG jointly sponsored the psychic Uri Geller with the University Lecture Series.

title: Marshall Tucker Band is upstaged by Freddie King
body: ASG brought the Marshall Tucker Band to Diddle Arena on Monday 8 April 1974, with Freddie King leading in. The Talisman said King, brought back for encores by a screaming crowd, was the biggest crowd pleaser, while Diddle's acoustics destroyed much of Marshall Tucker's set and the disappointed crowd began drifting towards the doors halfway through.

title: Kool and the Gang announced to close the year
body: The Herald previewed boogie and bluegrass coming to campus, and the Talisman recorded that the soul show band Kool and the Gang was scheduled to close out ASG's year alongside a festival set for 27 April. Neither source confirms that either event took place.

title: Student-Faculty Interaction seminars
body: ASG set up a series of informative seminars under a Student-Faculty Interaction Program, run with the undergraduate advisement office. The programmes were informal meetings between students and department representatives to discuss possible majors, aimed at students who had not decided.

title: Steve Henry resigns the discount post
body: The Herald reported that Steve Henry had resigned his ASG discount post. Henry was elected ASG president a year later and ran on a platform of entertainment and student services.

title: Rain drives the Bluegrass Festival indoors
body: ASG sponsored a Bluegrass Festival on 28 August 1974, headlined by Lester Flatt and the Clinch Mountain Clan, who described their music as folk music with overdrive. Scheduled as an outdoor festival in the amphitheatre, it had to be moved into Van Meter Auditorium because of rain.

title: A $42,000 entertainment budget, $27,000 of it for two free concerts
body: ASG operated on a budget of $42,000 for all forms of entertainment in 1974-75. It set aside $27,000 for two free concerts and $15,000 for mini-concerts, dances and other acts, with major concerts financed by their own gate receipts.
money: $42,000 entertainment budget; $27,000 for two free concerts, $15,000 for mini-concerts and dances

title: Students picket the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert
body: Doc Severinsen played the Homecoming concert on 11 October 1974 with Today's Children and the Now Generation Brass, before roughly 3,000 people, a substantial majority of them alumni. About thirty students picketed the doors; Severinsen complimented the audience for braving the picket lines and said he respected the demonstrators' right to exercise an American privilege.

title: Protest produces a coalition for change in concert booking
body: The Herald reported that the protest at the Severinsen concert had prompted a coalition seeking change in concert booking. The Student Action Committee that resulted argued that Ron Beck did not have the time the booking job needed and sought power for the activities vice president to negotiate with acts; Kentucky law prevented a student from controlling the funds, so the role stayed advisory, and the committee later folded into ASG's Student Activities Committee.

title: Barefoot Jerry costs ASG almost $1,500
body: The Nashville group Barefoot Jerry entertained a small crowd in Van Meter with a set that ranged across rock, country, blues and jazz and ended in a standing ovation. Activities vice president Tom LaCivita said ASG lost almost $1,500 on it; the Talisman, which does not date the show, called it one of the finer shows of its size at Western.

title: Al Stewart's mini-concert dies with his US tour
body: ASG booked Al Stewart for a mini-concert on 3 November 1974, but his United States tour was cancelled over immigration law. Tom LaCivita booked Kiss in his place, in an effort to ease the pressure students had put on ASG over its choice of acts.

title: America plays free and pushes ASG further into debt
body: ASG presented America as the first free concert of the school year on 7 November 1974, with Chad Stewart of Chad and Jeremy opening. Cracked speakers and feedback marred the sound, but lighters brought the band back for 'A Horse with No Name'; the Talisman recorded that ASG went into steadily increasing debt by presenting America free.

title: ASG establishes a service area
body: Jim Reynolds reported in the Herald that ASG had established a service area. The reorganisation of that year had put ASG's work into two areas, student affairs and academic affairs, with projects assigned to one or the other.

title: Kiss plays Van Meter and Ron Beck swears off the genre
body: Kiss played to a capacity crowd in Van Meter Auditorium on 7 December 1974, with smoke bombs, fire-eating, whiteface and leather bat wings, and Gene Simmons simulating vomiting and dripping stage blood over the front row. Ron Beck said afterwards that he would never again take part in booking this kind of act for Western because the show had no educational value for students.

title: War and the Charlie Daniels Band open warfare in Diddle
body: ASG's first major spring concert put War and the Charlie Daniels Band in Diddle Arena on 3 March 1975. Students called the Charlie Daniels set the best they had had in years and matches and lighters brought him back for 'Orange Blossom Special', but attendance was very low.

title: Bookstore prices cut and a part-time athletic discount approved
body: The Herald reported in the same issue that an ASG move had cut bookstore prices, that a part-time athletic discount had been approved and that the Volunteer Bureau had been made part of ASG. ASG had proposed raising the part-time incidental fee so part-time students could enter athletic events on the same footing as full-time students.

title: Volunteer Bureau and tutorial programme absorbed into ASG
body: The Student Volunteer Bureau, which placed students in community volunteer work, was weakened when founder Rodney Berry could not secure administrators or funds. Berry approached president Jeff Consolo about folding it into ASG, and the merger passed at the last meeting of the fall semester by better than 80 per cent; the tutorial programme was consolidated into ASG at the same time.

title: A better and cheaper student discount card
body: ASG changed the student discount card for what the Talisman described as a far better and cheaper one. The change was listed among the accomplishments of the Consolo administration alongside the new academic complaint system.

title: Regents add $16,000 to the entertainment budget and buy a second free concert
body: The Board of Regents passed a $16,000 increase in the ASG entertainment budget in August 1975. President Steve Henry said the increase allowed a second free concert and that he had never known one year to have two free concerts, much less two in a semester.
money: $16,000 increase in the ASG entertainment budget

title: Gove, Alex Harvey and Bottom and Company welcome students back
body: Two free concerts opened the fall semester to welcome students back, featuring Gove, Alex Harvey and Bottom and Company at the fine arts centre outdoor theatre. Harvey picked a dulcimer with a feather during his set.

title: ASG sponsors LAMB, a messianic music duo
body: On 11 September 1975 ASG sponsored LAMB, a duo specialising in messianic music, in Van Meter Auditorium. The Talisman noted the concert was well attended, perhaps because many students had writing assignments for MC 272 classes that required it.

title: Loggins and Messina open the season and lose $7,000
body: Kenny Loggins and Jim Messina played the first major concert of the year in Diddle Arena on Wednesday 17 September 1975, with the Amazing Rhythm Aces also on the bill. The crowd of 4,300 was too small and ASG lost about $7,000; activities vice president Rick Kelley blamed a lack of student body support.

title: Jules Bergman speaks on '2000 A.D. - The Way it Will Be'
body: ABC science editor Jules Bergman came to campus on 23 September 1975 for the first guest of the University Lecture Series, which the Talisman notes was also sponsored by ASG. Poor weather hurt the crowd; Bergman said man was adaptable enough to fly to the moon six times but could not endure much longer what he had created for himself on earth.

title: Doug Kershaw takes three encores in Homecoming week
body: ASG brought the Cajun fiddler Doug Kershaw for the Thursday night of Homecoming week, 30 October 1975. About 700 people saw him jump into the crowd to lead 'Jambalaya' and land in the lap of a startled coed in the fourth row; he took three encores and closed with 'Louisiana Man'.

title: Pat Paulsen returns for a free 'Lecture in Humor'
body: Pat Paulsen entertained a Diddle Arena crowd on Homecoming eve, 31 October 1975, at a free show sponsored by ASG. Presenting 'A Lecture in Humor', he traced the history of comedy from prehistoric times to the future and said he had found out you cannot speak your mind and expect to get elected.

title: ASG creates a student activities committee for concerts, lectures and publicity
body: To settle the dispute over booking, ASG adopted a Student Activities Committee, put into operation on 2 December 1975 and chaired by Rick Kelley. From 63 applicants, 17 members were chosen across three subcommittees, seven for concerts, five for lectures and five for publicity, each with alternates.

title: Oliver and Jerico Harp play free to a sparse crowd
body: A sparse crowd attended the Oliver and Jerico Harp concert on Wednesday 3 December 1975. The Talisman described it as a freebie to students.

title: ASG and Veterans on Campus run a book exchange against the bookstore
body: To give students an alternative to the College Heights Bookstore, ASG co-sponsored a book exchange with Veterans on Campus from 12 to 26 January 1976. Administrative vice president Christy Vogt said the two groups had covered expenses by 21 January through the sale of over 600 books, with ASG and VOC making 25 cents on each book sold.
money: over 600 books sold; 25 cents profit per book

title: A second campus check-cashing facility opens after an ASG survey
body: An ASG survey at fall registration found that the most significant desire of students was a new check-cashing facility. A second campus check-cashing point opened in the customer service area of the bookstore on 26 January 1976 for nine hours a week, after the original proposal for a full-service campus bank branch was judged impractical by area bankers.

title: The Spinners and Wet Willie draw 7,500 to a free concert
body: The free concert by the Spinners and Wet Willie on 30 January 1976 attracted 7,500 people, the second straight major ASG promotion to make money. The Spinners impersonated the Ink Spots, the Mills Brothers, Tom Jones, the Miracles and Elvis Presley and donned wigs for the Supremes; it was the first concert the new Student Activities Committee helped bring about.

title: George Allen lectures on success and ambition
body: George Allen, head coach of the Washington Redskins, spoke in the Garrett Conference Center on 12 February 1976 in one of the spring ASG-sponsored lectures. He showed a film, answered questions on professional football and advised those facing a tight job market that the last thing to talk about when looking for a job is money.

title: Chris Miller of National Lampoon draws 1,100 and a rebuke from the dean
body: Chris Miller of National Lampoon drew about 1,100 people to the Garrett Conference Center on 24 February 1976 with a lecture titled 'Toe Sucking in Albania, or An Evening of Erotic Laughter'. Three days later the Herald reported that dean of student affairs Charles Keown had criticised ASG's taste in sponsoring the lecture.

title: George Wallace is fought over in committee and never appears
body: President Steve Henry reported a 99 per cent chance of getting George Wallace, then seeking the Democratic presidential nomination, to speak in April 1976. A subcommittee of ASG's Student Activities Committee voted 4-2 with one abstention on 6 February to strike Wallace from the list of lecturers on the grounds that the arrangements had been made improperly, ASG Congress overruled the resolution, and by 13 February the Herald reported the lecture was uncertain; no appearance is recorded.

title: Truman Capote lectures off the cuff
body: Truman Capote lectured on 21 April 1976. The Herald's account two days later reported that off-the-cuff remarks were the highlight.

title: ASG plans an activities grand finale
body: The Herald reported that ASG was planning an activities grand finale to end the year. The fortnight that followed carried the Truman Capote lecture, two teacher forums and the free James Taylor concert.

title: ASG to sponsor two teacher forums
body: The Herald reported that ASG would sponsor two teacher forums. They came at the end of a year in which ASG had also pushed through the academic complaint system.

title: ASG's own supplement counts the discount cards and the book exchange
body: In the Student Insight supplement it paid for and wrote itself, ASG set out its services for the year: the discount cards it sponsored, the book exchange run with Veterans on Campus which it called a success, and its work on laundry facilities and intramural facilities. Christy Vogt wrote the piece on laundry improvements and Elaine Boeckman the piece on the abolition of women's hours.

title: Laundry improvements take effect
body: From 15 April 1976 the university installed more washers and dryers, an air-conditioned study area and a laundry pick-up service, with dry cleaning by a local firm in the proposal. Steve Henry said he hoped the facilities, which ASG had proposed the previous October, would be long-lasting.

title: ASG and the Center Board publish the 1976-77 events schedule
body: The summer Herald carried the University Center Board and ASG schedule of events for 1976-77. By late August the Herald was reporting two lectures and two concerts on ASG's entertainment slate and that ASG was seeking an appearance by Chicago.

title: Lori Wolfson opens the mini-concert series
body: ASG continued its mini-concert series with the acoustic guitarist Lori Wolfson in Van Meter Auditorium on 10 September 1976. The second, on 22 September, was Jerico Harp, whose Jim Thomas and Tom Schmidt mixed their own material with songs including Dan Fogelberg's 'Wysteria'.

title: 400 books sold in the ASG and Veterans on Campus co-op
body: The Herald reported that 400 books had been sold in the book co-op ASG ran with Veterans on Campus. The exchange had been advertised in the first issue of the year.

title: Students petition for their Maranatha concert money back
body: Students petitioned ASG for the return of a concert payment connected with the Maranatha Christian Center. ASG voted to refund the Maranatha money on 1 October, and by 8 October the Herald reported the Judicial Council had dropped the ASG-Maranatha case.

title: Bob Woodward cancels and comes six months late
body: Carl Bernstein was booked to open the lecture season but contracted pneumonia, and his partner Bob Woodward was announced as a substitute before cancelling his Western and University of Kentucky dates for work. Promoters paid the advertising costs for the cancelled lecture, but someone in the ASG office drew a bull's-eye on Woodward's publicity poster; he finally appeared in early April 1977.

title: Chicago grosses $53,092 and becomes Western's most successful concert
body: Chicago appeared at Diddle Arena on 15 October 1976, drew 10,450 people and grossed $53,092, the most financially successful concert Western had staged. The show cost $25,000 and was promoted by Reggae Ltd of St Louis with ASG, the first privately promoted concert at Western; about 5,000 advance tickets were sold, another record, and Ron Beck called it one of the best the university had ever had.

title: Seals and Crofts play Homecoming and lose $3,800
body: Jim Seals and Dash Crofts returned to Western for the Homecoming concert on Saturday 6 November 1976, with the Cate Brothers opening. About 5,200 attended and the concert lost roughly $3,800; Ron Beck blamed the Saturday date, saying everyone was worn out from the rest of Homecoming day. Afterwards the pair held a fireside chat with about 80 students about their Baha'i faith.

title: ASG Homecoming dance with the Back Stabbers and Those Perfections
body: For those who wanted livelier Homecoming entertainment, ASG sponsored a dance in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom featuring the Back Stabbers and Those Perfections. It ran the same weekend as the Seals and Crofts concert.

title: Barry Manilow plays free to 7,000 and cuts his set short
body: Barry Manilow gave the only free major concert of the semester on Monday 15 November 1976 before 7,000 people. The show cost $23,000, with ticket sales subtracting $10,100 from that; a heckler on the first row put Manilow in a bad mood, so he dropped his commercial set and cut the show by fifteen minutes.
money: cost $23,000, less $10,100 in ticket sales; attendance 7,000

title: Clive Barnes, John Sears and Vincent Bugliosi on the lecture series
body: The lecture season carried Clive Barnes of the New York Times in early November on 'The Plight of the Theatre Today', John Sears, Nixon's 1968 campaign manager and later Reagan's, in late November, and Vincent Bugliosi, the Manson prosecutor and author of 'Helter Skelter', in early December. Members of the ASG lecture committee, David Carwell, Ricky Sheppard and Mike Seiler, hosted the visiting speakers.

title: David Frye fills Van Meter with impersonations of Nixon
body: The comedian David Frye kept a capacity crowd in Van Meter Hall laughing in mid-September 1976 with impersonations of political figures and film stars, Richard Nixon foremost among them. In January the comedian Robert Klein warmed about 700 people in the Garrett Conference Center ballroom in arctic weather.

title: ASG considers cutting off the Volunteer Bureau
body: The Herald reported that ASG might discontinue funding for the Student Volunteer Bureau. A week later an editorial argued the bureau should have ASG's support; ASG kept funding it for another year before stopping in May 1978.

title: Book exchange sells more than 1,100 books
body: The Herald reported that the book exchange had sold more than 1,100 books. It was the strongest showing yet for the co-op ASG ran with Veterans on Campus.

title: Ethos returns for a Valentine's Day mini-concert
body: Ethos appeared on Valentine's Day 1977 in ASG's mini-concert series. The band had first played Western as an ASG mini-concert in October 1973.

title: Rufus and Wild Cherry draw 6,500 to a loud spring show
body: Rufus and Wild Cherry headlined the first major spring concert on 23 March 1977, opened by Fresh, whom Ron Beck signed for $500 because they were a favourite of Wild Cherry. About 6,500 attended, roughly 4,000 of them students, and Chaka Khan sang on her birthday; Beck said students told him the concert was too loud and that Rufus did not perform to their expectations.
money: attendance about 6,500; opening act Fresh cost $500

title: Student discount card covers 29 merchants
body: The Herald reported that the student discount card offered reductions from 29 merchants. The same issue carried Rick Kelley's review of a year in which Chicago and Barry Manilow headlined the concerts and a prosecutor and a reporter were among the speakers.

title: ASG books its first show of the year
body: The Herald reported in the first issue of the year that ASG had booked its first show. The same freshman issue advertised a used book exchange scheduled in West Hall.

title: Waylon Jennings plays after a cocaine arrest scare
body: Waylon Jennings and Jessi Colter opened the concert year on 9 September 1977 before about 5,000 people. Jennings and his secretary had been arrested in Nashville on a charge of conspiring to possess cocaine and some feared the show would be cancelled, but he was permitted to keep the date; Colter opened with a thirty-minute set before the band Waylon took over.

title: ASG proposes a campus shuttle bus
body: An ASG proposal said a shuttle bus was needed to relieve crowded parking lots. The Herald had editorialised a month earlier that a shuttle bus was the best answer to the parking problem.

title: Charlie Daniels rescues Homecoming after the Atlanta Rhythm Section cancels
body: The Atlanta Rhythm Section cancelled its Homecoming concert, and the Charlie Daniels Band came to Western's rescue on Homecoming eve, Thursday 27 October 1977. Daniels was promoting 'Midnight Wind' and played 'Long-Haired Country Boy', 'The South's Gonna Do It Again' and 'Orange Blossom Special'; ARS rescheduled for February.

title: Celebrity Ball plays the ASG Homecoming dance
body: Celebrity Ball, a rock group from Atlanta, entertained at an ASG-sponsored dance in the Garrett Conference Ballroom on Homecoming night, after the 20-20 tie with Morehead before an estimated 19,750 fans. It was the fiftieth Homecoming since Henry Hardin Cherry conceived the tradition in 1927.

title: Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins lose $13,200
body: Only 2,916 came to see Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins in Diddle Arena on 8 November 1977, a concert that cost the university about $31,200. The Herald reported a loss of $13,200; both men were riding new gold albums, Mason took one encore and Loggins three, and the shortfall nearly eliminated the free spring concert.

title: The book swap is called off for the spring
body: The Herald reported that the book swap was off for the spring semester. The same issue carried ASG's plans for its spring activities and a bill to support a state landlord-tenant measure.

title: Few tickets sold for the Atlanta Rhythm Section
body: The Herald reported that few tickets had been sold for the ASG concert by the Atlanta Rhythm Section. The warning proved accurate a week later.

title: Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick lose $12,000 on Valentine's Day
body: The Atlanta Rhythm Section finally appeared on 14 February 1978, bringing fellow Atlantans Brick, who opened with 'Dazz' and 'Dusic'. Most of the audience left before ARS took the stage; only 2,346 tickets were sold and the university lost about $12,000. United Black Students had announced in January that it would help arrange for Brick and LTD to appear, but LTD did not.

title: Average White Band signed for the free concert
body: The Herald reported that groups had been signed for the free ASG concert, with the Average White Band on the bill. ASG had said in February that its losses would not halt the free concert.

title: Average White Band and the Ramsey Lewis Trio close the year free, and draw 3,300
body: The free spring concert on 18 April 1978 put the Average White Band and the Ramsey Lewis Trio in Diddle Arena and drew about 3,300, ASG's last show of the year. The Scottish group charged $10,000 and the talent fee for the Ramsey Lewis Trio was $5,000; the Herald's reviewer wrote that the band made a concerted effort but the fans were few.
money: AWB fee $10,000; Ramsey Lewis Trio fee $5,000; attendance about 3,300

title: Grandpa Jones and Lester Flatt at the Bluegrass Festival
body: Grandpa Jones entertained a crowd at the fine arts center amphitheatre during an ASG-sponsored Bluegrass Festival in the spring of 1978, with the Pinnacle Boys and Lester Flatt and the Nashville Grass also on the programme. The Herald reported on 25 April that the bluegrass crowds were relaxed and casual.

title: $23,000 of losses nearly cost ASG the concert programme
body: After ASG lost more than $23,000 on major concerts across the year, dean of student affairs Charles Keown recommended to the Board of Regents that its entertainment budget be halved for 1978-79 and that a committee study whether the University Center Board should take over programming. Bob Moore argued at the 29 April meeting that students would have less involvement if the change were made, and the regents voted to let ASG keep its full $62,000 entertainment budget while directing President Downing to appoint the study committee.
money: more than $23,000 lost on major concerts; $62,000 entertainment budget retained for 1978-79

title: ASG stops funding the Volunteer Bureau and starts a newsletter
body: The Herald reported that ASG had stopped funding the Student Volunteer Bureau and would start a newsletter. The bureau, which placed students in community volunteer work and in elementary school tutoring, had been part of ASG since January 1975.

title: ASG hands its concerts to an outside promoter
body: The Board of Regents gave ASG authority to seek outside help booking concerts, and ASG contracted Sunshine Promotions of Indianapolis, producers of a Rolling Stones show in Lexington that summer and of Summer Jam II in Louisville. The firm had booked more than 150 concerts; for its part of the bargain ASG was to receive 13 percent of the net profits. President Steve Thornton said at least three major concerts were being planned for the year.
money: ASG to take 13 percent of net profits

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 5, 7 September 1978

title: Player and Exile play the Homecoming concert
body: Player and Exile played Diddle Arena on Homecoming night to 4,296 people. Player, whose hits were "This Time I'm In It For Love" and "Baby Come Back," failed to get the crowd on its feet; Exile, from Richmond, skipped its sound check and played through poor sound but had the arena standing. After $24,000 in production costs and Western's 13 percent cut of a $25,694.29 after-tax gross, the Talisman recorded that there was little financial success to speak of.
money: $25,694.29 after-tax gross; $24,000 production costs; Western took 13 percent

title: The Herald tells ASG to quit the concert business
body: An unsigned Herald editorial said it was time ASG got out of the concert business, arguing that concert promotion had taken most of the organisation's time and effort and that ASG could not even hire a promoter competently. It cited excessive university demands, poor communication with Sunshine Promotions and the unsigned contract behind the Homecoming show. The same issue carried a reader's letter defending the concert as good.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 23, 9 November 1978

title: Joe Cocker drops out; Wet Willie takes his place
body: Joe Cocker, who had been announced to appear with the Outlaws at Diddle Arena on 5 December, cancelled his entire tour, and Sunshine Promotions signed the southern rock band Wet Willie in his place. Advertisements in that issue read "ASG and WKU Present" the Outlaws with special guest Wet Willie, 7:30 p.m., $6 in advance and $7 on the day of the show. The same meeting heard that Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, would speak on 7 December in Van Meter Auditorium.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 27, 28 November 1978

title: The Outlaws cancel after 242 tickets sell
body: Reaction to the advertising for the Outlaws and Wet Willie was so poor that only 242 tickets had been sold by the week of the show. When the Outlaws' manager heard the figure he cancelled on the spot, according to university programs coordinator Tim Nemeth. The December date, ASG's replacement for the Joe Cocker booking, never happened.

title: John Prine sells out Van Meter and ASG still loses $2,000
body: John Prine came to Western in the autumn of 1978 and did what no other musical act had done in a long time, playing to a capacity house. But Van Meter Auditorium holds only slightly more than 1,000, and even with a sellout and tickets priced higher than any previous mini-concert, ASG lost about $2,000 on the show. His five-man band ran through 25 songs, among them "Spanish Pipedream," "Dear Abby," "The Bottomless Lake" and "Sam Stone."

title: Eleanor Smeal's lecture keeps slipping
body: Activities vice president David Carwell told ASG's first meeting of the semester that the university was still trying to reschedule a lecture by Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, for February or March; she had been announced for 7 December and had not come. He set out what ASG was paying the three speakers it had signed: $4,000 for Dick Gregory, $2,000 for Princeton professor Gerard O'Neill and $2,000 for Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm, plus expenses, with all the lectures free. Carwell added that tickets for the Heart concert at Diddle Arena on 15 February would go on sale on 22 January at $7 in advance and $8 on the day.
money: Gregory $4,000; O'Neill $2,000; Chisholm $2,000; Heart tickets $7 advance, $8 day of show

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 33, 18 January 1979

title: Heart at Diddle Arena
body: Heart played Diddle Arena on 15 February with Ann Wilson opening on "High Times" and her sister Nancy on guitar, running through "Heartless," "Straight On," "Magazine," "Mistral Wind," "Dog and Butterfly," "Hijinx," "Crazy on You" and "Barracuda." Sunshine Promotions had signed the band as its first major break for Western, but only 5,821 came, a little more than half of capacity. Western made about $5,200 from the show, the one clear financial success of the concert year.

title: Forum '79 cut to one night
body: ASG's gubernatorial candidates' discussion panel, scheduled for two nights, was shortened to one after the university orchestra needed Van Meter Auditorium on the Monday. President Steve Thornton said the surviving session would run at 7:30 p.m. on the Tuesday, with Democrats Carroll Hubbard, Ralph Ed Graves and George Atkins appearing and Lieutenant Governor Thelma Stovall sending a representative. Ray White was the only Republican candidate willing to attend; Terry McBrayer and Louie Nunn stayed away.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 48, 27 March 1979

title: Regents take concerts and lectures away from ASG
body: On 31 March the Board of Regents approved moving the activities that ASG had run, lectures and concerts among them, to a rebuilt University Center Board and funded that board with $80,000 for programming from autumn 1979. The new committees were to include the ASG president, the activities vice president and one congress member alongside Greek, United Black Students, residence hall and faculty representatives. Programs coordinator Tim Nemeth said the new board would involve at most ten students in lectures and concerts where ASG had involved fifty.

title: ASG replaces concerts with opinion polls and a radio phone-in
body: Stripped of entertainment, ASG spent the year on student opinion polls, a phone-in programme on the campus station WKYU where President Jamie Hargrove answered questions, and expanded publicity for its own elections. Hargrove said the transfer of activities to the University Center Board had cost ASG between $60,000 and $70,000 of budget but no real power. Poll committee chairman Kevin Kinne said the university administration was showing a lot of support for the polls.
money: $60,000 to $70,000 of activities budget lost to the Center Board

title: ASG asks the bookstore to break even on books
body: ASG introduced a bill asking the College Heights Bookstore to adopt a break-even policy on book sales, arguing that the store had a monopoly on textbooks and that the College Heights Foundation which runs it is a non-profit organisation. Congress was to vote on it the following week. At the same meeting congress formed an ad hoc committee on university food services.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 55, No. 34, 31 January 1980

title: International Food Fest and fashion show
body: In the spring semester ASG followed International Week with an International Food Fest and fashion show. International students committee chairman Osama Shariff, a junior from Jerusalem, said attendance at the autumn programmes had been very good and that they were well put together. The Talisman called International Week the highlight of ASG's autumn semester.

title: ASG's car pool match-up
body: ASG ran a car pool match-up scheme jointly with the Barren River Area Development District and hoped to continue it. Almost 450 students took part across the two semesters. It was one of the few concrete services the organisation carried through in a year the Talisman headlined as a year of resolutions.

title: The discount cards that never existed
body: ASG announced it would file complaints with the Better Business Bureaus of Georgia and Texas against University Press Inc. of Lewisville, Texas, and Atlanta, which had taken $275 from each of at least four Bowling Green merchants for ASG-endorsed student discount cards that were never produced. A man calling himself Louis F. Cordoba had told Gary Smith of the Bouquet Shoppe on the U.S. 31-W By-Pass that then-president Steve Fuller had recommended his shop as an advertiser, and Smith wrote a $275 cheque on 18 March. The cards were supposed to have been handed out at registration for the autumn.
money: $275 taken from each of at least four merchants

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 5, 10 September 1981

title: 14,000 cards, a dead phone line and a returned letter
body: President Marcel Bush had spent three weeks trying to reach the company printing 14,000 ASG discount cards: the Texas number was disconnected, an answering service pushed her to an Atlanta number nobody answered, and a letter to the Texas address came back from the post office. On the day complaints were being filed, company representative Phil Bewley finally telephoned to say the cards had shipped from New York and that printing problems had caused the delay. The Herald noted that until two years earlier ASG had printed discount cards at its own expense as a free student service, charging merchants nothing, and had dropped it when costs became prohibitive.
money: 14,000 cards; merchants paid $275 for a listing

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 10, 29 September 1981

title: A volunteer student escort service
body: A student escort service jointly sponsored by Interhall Council, ASG and the university police began operating, walking women anywhere on campus from dark until midnight Sunday to Thursday on a single telephone number, with a vehicle in bad weather. Coordinator James Hunter said Western was the first university in the country with a completely volunteer, student-operated escort service, and that it had filled about 500 to 600 requests in its first year without a single incident. Public safety director Paul Bunch said requests for escorts had tripled after two students were raped the previous year.
money: 500 to 600 requests filled in the first year

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 58, No. 4, 2 September 1982

title: ASG prints the discount card itself
body: After an agreement collapsed with University Services Associates of St. Mary's, Missouri, ASG voted to print the student discount cards itself, and they were finally handed out in November through the Student Affairs and Public Relations committees working with Interhall Council. Nine businesses appeared on the card, among them the seven merchants who had paid company president George Wheaton for the original card and never got a refund. President Jack Smith said the businesses would have to recover their own money: "They got what they paid for. They got their discount card."
money: nine businesses on the card; seven merchants unrefunded

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 59, No. 23, 10 November 1983

title: ASG votes to study a book exchange
body: ASG voted to study the feasibility of a student book exchange and formed a committee to examine schemes at the universities of Louisville and Kentucky. Two models were discussed: a room where students sold and bought books at prices they set, and a cheaper list of students, telephone numbers, books for sale and asking prices. President Jack Smith said books were more expensive every year and students needed somewhere besides the College Heights Bookstore, adding, "I don't think there's anything wrong with a little competition."

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 7, 20 September 1984

title: Book exchange ambassadors work the campus
body: ASG sent "ambassadors" out to campus organisations to explain the new book exchange and hand out registration cards, with public relations vice president John Holland promising to send a speaker "faster than Domino's pizza." Registration cards went into campus mailboxes on 5 December and had to be returned by 21 December, with an off-campus coupon printed in the Herald. The list of available books was to be compiled over Christmas and published as a tabloid of names, telephone numbers and titles when students returned in January.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 24, 29 November 1984

title: The book exchanger's first edition
body: The tabloid book exchanger was distributed in the first week of the spring semester and students began telephoning each other to haggle over used textbooks. Committee co-chairmen John Holland and senior class president Danny Broderick, with President Jack Smith and administrative secretary Debra Stahl, keyed the entries into an IBM Personal Computer over the Christmas break on a program written for $25 by Bill Chestnut, a computer science graduate from Berea; Ginger Williams of the Franklin Favorite did the typesetting. Smith said the University of Kentucky had listed 700 books in its first exchange and Western had double that, and Broderick said ASG made no money from it: "This was a labor of love."
money: $25 paid for the computer program; about 1,400 books listed

title: ASG takes Big Brothers/Big Sisters children to a Lady Toppers game
body: Congress members each paired themselves with a child from Big Brothers/Big Sisters of Bowling Green for the women's last home basketball game, spending the evening counting heads, running trips to the bathroom and making enough noise to see the Lady Toppers past Cincinnati 122-72. Before the game the children ate snacks, made banners for the spirit contest and played pool and video games in the university center. The Herald reported that mothers in the crowd gave the student government members understanding looks.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 43, 5 March 1985

title: The commonwealth attorney is asked to find the discount card printer
body: ASG's student discount cards finally went out in October after Phil Bewley of Parkland Publishers Inc. missed two August deadlines and the Warren County Commonwealth Attorney's Office was called in to find him. Bewley, reached by telephone in Nashville, said he believed President Mitchell McKinney had understood the cards would not be ready until 23 September, and blamed printer trouble. It was the second time in five years the same representative had left an ASG discount card in limbo.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 61, No. 13, 10 October 1985

title: ASG wins its division of November Nonsense
body: ASG was the only non-Greek group to enter November Nonsense, the variety show Chi Omega has staged since 1965, and took first place in the organisation division. Its skit followed an orange-faced, loud-mouthed "oompah" projected from 1965, when he was a star Western footballer, to 1985, when he became a potential candidate for the university presidency. Seven groups performed four-to-six minute skits on a "Back to the Future" theme, and the sorority raised about $800 for Hospice.

title: ASG hosts the state student government conference
body: ASG hosted the state Student Government Conference at Glasgow to promote involvement and the role of student government. President Mitchell McKinney and the organisation's roughly 100 members also joined the students, faculty and administrators who rallied in Frankfort in support of higher education in Kentucky. McKinney sat on the University Center Board and the Education Advisory Committee as well as the Board of Regents.

title: ASG asks for lights in 11 dark spots
body: After two women were assaulted within a fortnight in April, ASG passed a resolution on 10 April asking for more lighting in eleven places on campus. A Herald editorial on 15 April backed it, noting that a new lamppost cost between $500 and $750 and about $36.50 a year to run, "a small price to pay for safety." The same spring saw more women using the escort service and enrolling in the university's self-defence class.
money: $500 to $750 per lamppost; about $36.50 a year to run

title: A state association floated as the route to better entertainment
body: The first Herald of the Associated Students' first full year carried an article headed "Campus Entertainment Improvements Possible Through State Association," the earliest sign of the block-booking idea that would define the organisation's entertainment work for the next decade. The same issue announced Jesse Stuart lecturing on campus and ran the paper's regular Marquee film column.

title: A monthly events calendar posted outside the Associated Students office
body: The Herald reported that the month's campus events were being posted outside the Associated Students office. It is the earliest standing service the record shows the new government running for students.

title: A student writes in wanting more entertainment
body: Tony Burdoc's letter, headed "Wants More Entertainment," ran in the Herald in April 1967, part of a running complaint about what the year-old government was putting on. The same issue reported that bluegrass and folk music would be the theme of Western's first Lost River Festival.

title: The case for a student book exchange
body: Mark Dossey reported in the Herald that student book exchanges were working at Murray State and the University of Louisville, an argument for Western to run one of its own. Through the rest of the decade the exchange on this campus was run by the Veterans Club, not by the Associated Students.

title: The Associated Student Government sets its events for the year
body: The first Herald of 1967-68 announced the Associated Student Government's schedule of events for the coming year alongside the university's own lecture series and the Community Concerts season. It was the first year the government published a programme in advance.

title: Student government sets new programmes
body: The Herald reported that the student government had set new programmes for the year, in the same issue that announced Buckminster Fuller would lecture on campus and that Homecoming queen voting was set for Thursday.

title: The Four Tops booked for the Tuesday after the election
body: The Herald announced a Four Tops concert on campus the following Tuesday. The same issue reported the Associated Student Government sponsoring a dance that Friday and a Herald editorial arguing that campus groups needed more opportunity to run money-making events.

title: The Herald says the praise for student government is deserved
body: A Herald editorial headed "Praise for Associated Student Government Well Deserved" ran in November 1967, an unusually warm note in a paper that spent most of the era complaining about what the government booked.

title: An assessment to pay for entertainment
body: The Herald reported that an assessment would provide funds for campus entertainment. It is the earliest reference in the archive to a dedicated student charge behind the Associated Students' concert and lecture booking; the article index does not give the amount.
money: amount not stated in the Herald's article index

title: Booking problems plague the entertainment calendar
body: Ellen Bennett reported that booking problems still plagued the Associated Students entertainment calendar. The same issue carried Alana White on the government's committees starting work and announced the Cinema Guild's season of art films.

title: An Associated Students dance, and a book exchange that was not theirs
body: The Herald announced an Associated Students dance for the next day. The same issue reported the Veterans book exchange a tremendous success, a reminder that the textbook service students used in these years was run by the veterans' club and not by student government.

title: Sam and Dave play campus on 3 December
body: Gail Barton reported in the Herald of 21 November that Sam and Dave would entertain on 3 December 1968. The same issue announced an Associated Students dance that Friday night and carried Bruce Tucker arguing that the lectures lacked spark and needed a student forum.

title: The Chattanooga Coachmen booked for an Associated Students dance
body: The Herald announced that an Associated Students dance would feature the Chattanooga Coachmen. The same issue reported James Farmer scheduled for the lecture series and the government's election set for the following Tuesday.

title: James Farmer speaks, a first for the lecture series
body: The Herald's election special edition of 25 March 1969 carried the notice "James Farmer Speaks Tonight." The paper had introduced the appearance the previous week under the headline "James Farmer Marks a First for Lectures"; the CORE founder was the first speaker of his kind the series had brought to the Hill.

title: Henry Mancini in concert
body: Alana White announced in the Herald of 17 April that Henry Mancini would appear in concert, and the issue of 24 April set the date for that Saturday. Gail Barton and Ellen Bennett reviewed it on 1 May under the headline "Concert Sets Mood of Delight."

title: A committee opens a study of the campus speaker policy
body: Bruce Tucker reported that a committee had undertaken a study of the campus speaker policy. The question of who could be invited to Western ran through the next two years and was settled by the Board of Regents in October 1970.

title: Senator Mike Gravel billed for a lecture
body: The Herald announced Senator Mike Gravel of Alaska billed for a campus lecture in the last weeks of Bill Straeffer's term. The same issue reviewed the year under the headline "Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement."

title: A book exchange runs at the start of term
body: The first Herald of 1969-70 reported that a book exchange was reducing costs for students and would close on Thursday. The same issue announced the year's lecture series and the 1969 Homecoming theme.

title: John Lyne questions the music preference poll
body: John Lyne, a year before he became president, wrote in the Herald that the Associated Students Congress's music preference poll needed closer examination. The same issue reported Congress dropping discussion of the survey's validity and an editorial warning the lecture series promised a lacklustre season.

title: Associated Students moves to boost the entertainment fare
body: The Herald reported the Associated Students moving to boost the entertainment on offer, and separately that the government's film showings were contributing an extra cultural dimension to campus. The same issue announced a new calendar to aid students and reported NBC's Chet Huntley might speak at Western.

title: A discount book for students
body: The Herald announced that the Associated Student Government would issue a discount book, and backed it with an editorial headed "Discount Offers More for Money." The same issue reported the Lettermen returning for a December concert.

title: Twenty-one merchants sign the discount programme
body: The Herald reported that twenty-one local merchants had signed with the discount programme and that the Associated Student Government and the merchants had reached a discount co-operation. The same issue carried Reginald Glass asking whether the government's entertainment was slanted.

title: Congress considers raising the semester head fee
body: The Herald reported the Associated Students considering a boost in the semester head fee, the charge that paid for its programme. The article index does not record the figure discussed.
money: proposed increase; amount not stated in the article index

title: Blood, Sweat and Tears signs an Associated Students contract
body: The Herald reported that Blood, Sweat and Tears had signed a contract with the Associated Students. It was the biggest booking the organisation had made to that point.

title: Blood, Sweat and Tears play, and the audience entertains the entertainers
body: The Herald of 21 April set the Blood, Sweat and Tears concert for that Saturday. The review a week later ran under the headline "Audience 'Entertains' Entertainers," the paper's verdict on how the night went.

title: An Associated Students dance from eight until midnight
body: The Herald announced an Associated Students dance running from 8 to 12 that night, alongside the Cinema '70 showing of "The Promoter."

title: A student discount card planned for the autumn
body: Don Smith reported in the Herald that a student discount card was planned for the fall term, the next step on from the discount book issued in November 1969.

title: Symposiums to seek the views of students
body: Lyda Parker reported that symposiums would seek students' views, and the following issue reported them set for the dormitories. On 20 March the Herald called the level of interest an encouraging sign, and on 27 March reported the symposiums had been very successful.

title: The folk festival returns on 16 April
body: The Herald announced that the folk festival would return on 16 April 1970. Tom Todd reported on 21 April that the Southern Folk Festival performers had met an enthusiastic reception.

title: Western hosts a conference on discount programmes
body: The summer Herald reported that the Associated Students would host a conference on discount programmes and that discount cards would be given out at fall registration. Western was by then teaching other Kentucky campuses how to run the scheme.

title: The discount card offers savings
body: Kaye Thomas reported in the Herald that the discount card offered savings to students. The card was handed out at registration and ran through the year; John Lyne's own account of his term said the discount programme with local merchants had been maintained.

title: Associated Students presents a documentary double feature
body: The Herald announced that the Associated Students would present documentaries in a double feature that night. It is the first clearly labelled film screening the government put on itself, separate from the subscription-based Cinema Guild.

title: The Ides of March draw a meagre crowd
body: The Herald of 29 September billed the Ides of March for that Saturday. Travis Witt's review on 6 October reported the concert had attracted a meagre crowd, one of several poor houses that made 1970-71 a difficult year for campus bookings.

title: The Regents put an open speaker policy into effect
body: Richard Morris reported that a unanimous vote from the Regents had put the new speaker policy into effect. John Lyne said afterwards that the push for an open speaker policy, from student demand through to implementation, had yielded results; it is what made the Kunstler and Devlin bookings possible.

title: Congress to show films for Halloween
body: The Herald reported the Associated Student Congress would show films for Halloween. The same issue carried a letter from Mania Ritter mourning the death of concerts on campus.

title: Dick Gregory speaks after a second test of the new speaker policy
body: David Sutherland announced in the Herald of 30 October that the civil rights comedian Dick Gregory would speak on Monday, under an editorial headed "Dick Gregory Go-Ahead Poses Second Test." Clark Hanes interviewed him on 3 November and Ernie Hearion reported his line that the fate and destiny of the nation depended on youth. The 1971 Talisman dates the appearance to 12 November; the Herald's own contemporaneous coverage places it at the start of the month.

title: The Temptations draw a capacity crowd
body: Mason Ralph announced in the Herald of 17 November that the Temptations would sing the next day. His review on 20 November reported the group drew a capacity crowd and the concert evoked mixed reactions; the 1971 Talisman said they kept a packed house hypnotised.
money: capacity crowd, per the Herald review

title: Ravi Shankar plays Western
body: Mason Ralph announced on 4 December that Ravi Shankar was coming that Wednesday, and the 8 December issue put the sitar player in the concert spotlight for the following night. Lyne cited Shankar as proof that the government was bringing names that were not of the top forty variety.

title: Julian Bond speaks on a Sunday
body: Clark Hanes reported in the Herald of 11 December that the Georgia legislator Julian Bond would speak that Sunday. The 1971 Talisman lists Bond on 13 December among the more controversial speakers the Associated Students brought to campus.

title: William Kunstler speaks after a delay
body: The Herald of 20 November 1970 had billed the Chicago Seven lawyer to speak that Monday; he did not appear until the new year. The paper announced on 29 January that Kunstler was set to speak, and Peggy Kirkpatrick's piece on 2 February headed "Courtroom Paladin to Speak Thursday" carried the date. The 1971 Talisman shows Lyne hosting him on campus.

title: Bernadette Devlin speaks on a Friday night
body: The Herald announced the Irish MP's lecture on 19 February, called her an Irish firebrand on 23 February, and ran "Irish Socialist Speaks Tonight" on the day itself. Her appearance and Kunstler's were funded by a lecture bill the Associated Student Congress passed the previous November.

title: Neil Diamond in concert
body: The Herald of 26 February announced that the pop vocalist Neil Diamond would present a concert that Thursday. The 1971 Talisman lists Diamond and the Trinidad-Tripoli Steel Band as the spring entertainment.

title: S. I. Hayakawa lectures
body: The Herald announced on 30 March that Dr S. I. Hayakawa would lecture that Thursday. The 1971 Talisman lists him with Kunstler and Devlin as the spring speakers the Associated Students had scheduled.

title: A weekly radio programme on the government's work
body: The 1971 Talisman reported that, to promote better communication between students and their government, Lyne set up a weekly radio programme to tell of the Associated Students' work. The Herald front page reproduced in the yearbook records him saying the programme could be started within the hour.

title: The Trinidad Steel Band and the Serendipity Singers
body: The Herald previewed the double bill on 14 September as "Folk Rock vs Steel Band in Thursday Concert" and Kim Weaver's review on 21 September was headed "Steel Band Betters Singers in Concert." The 1972 Talisman calls it the first major Associated Students sponsored concert of the year and says student requests had brought the steel band back for a second consecutive year.

title: Benjamin Spock, the first Associated Students speaker of the year
body: The Herald of 21 September announced Dr Benjamin Spock lecturing on campus that Thursday. The 1972 Talisman records that Spock, the first speaker sponsored by the Associated Students that year, attacked the United States role in Vietnam and drew a crowd of about 1,100.

title: Ike and Tina Turner headline Homecoming before about 12,000
body: The 1972 Talisman reports the Ike and Tina Turner Revue performing before an estimated crowd of 12,000 in Diddle Arena at the Homecoming concert, backed by the eight-member Kings of Rhythm. The Herald of 19 October ran "Concert Lovers Buoyed by Turnout for Ike & Tina Turner" alongside a letter from Phyllis Sower repulsed at the actions of a student at the Friday night concert. It was the high point of the Associated Students' concert year.
money: estimated crowd of 12,000 in Diddle Arena

title: A mock election for governor draws 1,175 votes
body: The Associated Students ran a mock gubernatorial election on 21 October 1971. The 1972 Talisman records that only 1,175 of Western's 11,000 students voted and that they elected the Republican Tom Emberton; the Herald reported the result on 22 October. Kentucky's voters chose Wendell Ford by a substantial margin on 2 November.

title: First Gear plays a mini-concert
body: The Herald of 22 October reported First Gear featured for a mini-concert. The 1972 Talisman shows Larnelle Harris of First Gear on stage at an Associated Students sponsored mini-concert; the Persuasions and Supa were among the other groups that autumn.

title: Supa brings a jamboree to Western
body: The Herald announced on 29 October that the Associated Students had set a mini-concert with Supa for the next day, and Roger Miller's review on 2 November was headed "Mini-Concert Doesn't Mean Mini-Talent." A letter from Brent Ferguson the same week praised the Associated Students mini-concerts.

title: The government goes after rock groups
body: Travis Witt reported in the Herald that the Associated Students were contacting rock groups. The 1972 Talisman names Leon Russell, Mountain, Alice Cooper and It's a Beautiful Day as the acts approached after students asked for bigger names.

title: Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas cancelled the day before the show
body: The Herald billed two rock groups for a 2 December Associated Students concert on 12 November and named Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas on 19 November. The 1972 Talisman records that on 2 December, the day before the engagement, student government leaders were forced to cancel because Mountain's lead singer Felix Pappalardi was ill. A letter from Terry Gatlin questioning the cancellation ran in the Herald of 10 December.

title: A surprise mini-concert with Friction
body: Roger Miller reported in the Herald that a surprise mini-concert on the Wednesday had hot music by Friction. It came the week after the Mountain and Black Oak Arkansas cancellation.

title: The Legal Rights Committee runs a symposium with lawyers
body: Stephanie Madison reported that the Associated Students Legal Rights Committee was planning a symposium with lawyers for 1 December. Carter Pence's report on 3 December, "Students Air Complaints at Symposium," covered the event.

title: The Cellar, the Associated Students teahouse, opens
body: Roger Miller announced the opening in the Herald under the headline "Another First: the Cellar, Associated Students Teahouse, Opens Friday." The paper covered it again a week later as "Cellar-Dwellers" and reported the campus teahouse stirred mixed emotions; by the end of April the Herald was calling it a dimly lit teahouse that outshone the government's other efforts. The 1972 Talisman describes it as a coffee house in West Hall.

title: A free calendar for students
body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students were offering a free calendar, and Joe Huggins announced it again on 21 January. The same issue reported the government scheduling lectures, concerts and a film series for the second semester.

title: Art Buchwald lectures
body: Roger Miller reported that the humour columnist Art Buchwald would lecture that night. The 1972 Talisman records his lecture as "Art Buchwald at Large" and says it combined personal anecdotes with political commentary; he stayed afterwards to talk with students.

title: James J. Kilpatrick speaks
body: Reginald Glass announced in the Herald that the syndicated columnist James J. Kilpatrick would speak that night. The 1972 Talisman records him describing the youth vote as a real problem for the Republicans.

title: The Associated Students movie series opens with King Kong
body: The Herald announced that the Associated Students movie series would open the next day with "King Kong," and an editorial three days later said the series could be a hit. The 1972 Talisman lists the Gaslight film series among the government's new entertainment; the Herald of 2 May had W. C. Fields in "The Flying Ace" set for Gaslight.

title: The Jake Jones mini-concert is cancelled
body: The Herald reported that the Associated Students had cancelled the Jake Jones mini-concert set for 29 January. The same issue carried a letter from Anthony Kinzel disconcerted with the government.

title: A cancelled Lennon and Ono screening brings a furious postbag
body: The Herald of 28 January had announced John Lennon and Yoko Ono films for the following week. On 4 February the paper printed three letters about the cancellation, one from a student who wanted to see the Lennon film and two headed "Disappointed at Film Cancellation" and "Furious at Film Cancellation," alongside Roger Miller reporting the Associated Students Congress reacting to censorship.

title: Norman Mailer lectures
body: Roger Miller announced in the Herald of 8 February that Norman Mailer's lecture was slated for the following night. The 1972 Talisman records the author and social critic telling his audience that amateurism was replacing professionalism.

title: Four sent to the entertainment conference
body: Jill Flanders reported that Reginald Glass, Mike Fiorella, Ron Beck and Jim Schmidt attended an entertainment conference. The 1972 Talisman explains the machinery behind the year's programme: Ron Beck was unit co-ordinator for the state branch of the National Entertainment Conference, ten schools were represented, the state body met on the Western campus in both semesters for programming workshops, and the three mini-concerts each semester were the result.

title: The Isaac Hayes concert is cancelled
body: Carter Pence reported the cancellation in the Herald of 18 February. The 1972 Talisman says the 17 February concert failed to materialise because Hayes was suffering from flu, and that he later contacted Western to reschedule.

title: Benjamin Mays on two decades of human rights
body: The Herald announced the black educator's lecture on 25 February and ran "Benjamin Mays Speaks Tonight" on 29 February. The 1972 Talisman gives his subject as "Two Decades of Human Rights"; the yearbook's caption says he spoke on 29 February while its running text says only that he was scheduled to.

title: Edwin Reischauer, former ambassador to Japan
body: The Herald announced that the former ambassador would speak that night. The same issue reported that the Associated Students would present "The Fantasticks" and carried an editorial headed "Herald Salutes Associated Students."

title: The Imperials play a mini-concert
body: The Herald of 11 April announced that the Thursday Associated Students mini-concert would feature the Imperials.

title: The Carpenters in Diddle Arena
body: The Herald of 14 April announced that the Carpenters would appear in concert the following Tuesday. The 1972 Talisman confirms the brother and sister recording act appeared in Diddle Arena on 18 April; they had been promised to students back in October alongside Mountain, Black Oak Arkansas and Isaac Hayes.

title: It's a Beautiful Day and If close the concert year
body: The Herald of 20 April announced a rock concert for the following Thursday with It's a Beautiful Day and If. Reginald Glass wrote the preview "Beautiful Day, If Headline Concert" in the issue of 25 April.

title: The Cellar finishes the year the best thing the government did
body: The Herald of 28 April reported the Cellar's finals were set and ran a piece headed "Cellar: It's Only a Dimly Lit Teahouse but Outshines Other Associated Student Government Efforts." The same issue reported a concert highlighting the Folk Arts Festival and the installation of next year's officers.

title: Finances and scheduling name the problem
body: The Herald ran a piece headed "Finances, Scheduling Pose Problems in Entertainment" in the week of Homecoming. Over the following month the paper printed an editorial arguing the benefits outweighed the risks in scheduling big concerts and letters from students wanting bigger concerts and disputing the paper's handling of the entertainment question.

title: ASG takes over the student discount card
body: Associated Student Government took production of the wallet-sized student discount card in house after the company contracted the previous year delayed distribution. The printer, John Bewley, had been indicted by a Warren County grand jury for theft of service over $100 for failing to pay ASG the $500 it was owed for distributing the cards, then paid and had the case dismissed. Administrative vice president Lori Scott said about 20 merchants had already bought advertising at $100 each and she hoped for 30 to 40, with the cards out by the first week of October.
money: $100 per merchant advertisement, about 20 sold; a $500 debt recovered from the previous printer

title: Weekend in the Woods, the fourth annual ASG leadership camp
body: ASG sponsored the fourth annual Weekend in the Woods, a leadership conference at Camp Decker about 13 miles from Bowling Green, and 45 students attended against accommodation for 75 at $30 a head covering meals and lodging. Members had begun lining up speakers and camp reservations the previous March; seminars covered leadership, goal setting, generating ideas and listening, and for the first time student leaders spoke alongside faculty. State senator-elect Nick Kafoglis lectured, and when President Kern Alexander could not make the closing session he invited every Weekender to breakfast at his home a week later. The yearbook does not date the weekend.

src.label: 1987 Talisman, 'Branching Out - Weekend in the Woods'

title: $10,000 for campus lights and a plan for a student hangout
body: The 1987 Talisman recorded ASG's two main projects of the year as more campus lighting and a student hangout in Downing University Center, both traced to President Kern Alexander's concern about student retention raised at a September breakfast with ASG members. ASG persuaded the administration to put up $10,000 for new lights. To stop students going home at weekends, members formed committees to arrange the music and the lighting for a place in the university center where students could dance without leaving campus.
money: $10,000 from the administration for new campus lighting

title: A recorded campus events phone line is put on hold
body: A proposal to start a telephone service playing recorded messages about campus events was tabled at the 3 February meeting until more research could be done. The equipment would have cost $500, with $60 for installation and a $17 monthly service charge, and author Bill Schilling said promotion would add $200 more. Public Information director Fred Hensley had not been consulted before the bill was introduced, and the sports information office already ran a line of its own.
money: $500 equipment, $60 installation, $17 a month, plus $200 promotion

title: The Book Exchanger gets a third semester and a warning
